planting.note: Plant tubers or divisions after soil has warmed in spring; growth emerges late, so mark the spot to avoid disturbing dormant crowns.

directions: This selection of hardy begonia carries wing-shaped leaves that are dark green above and saturated with deep claret-red beneath, giving the whole clump a wine-toned glow when backlit. Loose, arching sprays of pale pink flowers dangle above the foliage on reddish stems from late summer into fall. Like the species it dies to the ground after frost and self-sows tiny bulbils along the stems, so extra plants appear readily the following spring. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled or afternoon shade alongside hostas and ferns.

planting.note: Set out divisions or potted-up bulbils in spring once frost danger passes; this clone breaks dormancy on the later side.

directions: Collected from a cold part of Japan, this exceptionally hardy form of hardy begonia has olive-green, heart-shaped leaves with red undersides and red-veined stems that catch evening light. Clusters of small pink-to-white flowers appear from late summer into fall on plants that reliably outsize the typical species. It is among the most cold-tolerant hardy begonia selections available, worth trying a zone colder than the straight species. Provide moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade.

planting.note: Divide or transplant in spring; forms a bushy mound that pairs well with hostas and ferns.

directions: Collected by plantsman Dan Hinkley in Japan, this hardy begonia bears green-backed leaves and is prized for pendulous flower clusters up to a foot long, far larger than the typical species. Rich pink blooms dangle from branching, pinkish-red stems from midsummer into fall, creating a fountain-like display. Small bulbils drop from the leaf axils in autumn and self-propagate readily. Best in organically rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in part to full shade.

planting.note: Cut to the ground after frost; new growth emerges from the crown and self-sown bulbils in late spring.

directions: Selected from seedlings of 'Heron's Pirouette', this hardy begonia forms wide clumps of upright, green-leaved stalks topped with pendulous spikes of bright pink flowers. Bloom is unusually long-lasting, running from June through September rather than the brief late-summer show typical of the species. It spreads wider than most hardy begonia selections, making it useful as a bold woodland-edge groundcover. Grow in bright shade with even moisture and rich, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant runners or rooted plantlets in spring; spreads readily by red thread-like stolons.

directions: Collected on Honshu, Japan, this strawberry saxifrage forms neat rosettes of rounded, hairy leaves that are purple-green overlaid with wine-red flushing in spring, deepening the coloring found in the species. It spreads by wiry red stolons that root at the tips, quickly forming a low patch useful for edging shaded beds or spilling from containers. Airy sprays of small white flowers with asymmetric petals rise above the foliage in late spring. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist soil protected from hot afternoon sun.

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring; establishes slowly and resents summer drought.

directions: This robust ligularia forms a broad clump of large, paddle-shaped, lobed leaves distinct from the rounder foliage of dentata types, giving it a coarser, more architectural presence in the border. Branching terminal racemes of yellow to orange daisy-like flowers rise well above the foliage in summer. Unlike shadier ligularia relatives, it tolerates more midday sun where soil stays consistently moist. Best sited in deep, fertile, reliably moist soil near a pond edge or in a boggy border, sheltered from drying wind.

planting.note: Transplant dormant rhizome divisions in early spring into leafy, humus-rich woodland soil.

directions: Native across western and northern North America, this fairybells species sends up unbranched or lightly branched stems clothed in alternate, parallel-veined leaves. Small, pale greenish-white bell flowers dangle singly or in pairs beneath the foliage in spring, followed by berries that ripen through yellow and orange to red. It naturalizes gradually by rhizomes in deep shade beneath conifers or deciduous canopy, making it a good companion for trilliums and native ferns. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil and undisturbed shade.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant divisions after last frost; mulch crowns for winter protection at the cold end of its range.

directions: A variegated selection of Chinese fairy bells found in nursery stock, this cultivar has silvery-white and green variegation radiating through each leaf, flushing with purple-pink tones as nights cool in autumn. Graceful arching bamboo-like stems emerge in spring, followed by small clusters of pale flowers in late spring and blue-black berries later in the season. Its variegation reads as a bright accent against dark-leaved shade companions like hellebores or heucheras. Grow in evenly moist, well-drained soil in dappled shade to part sun.
